client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away a few weeks ago. I keep losing focus at work — like, I'll be in the middle of something and suddenly I just can't remember what I was doing, or I'll find myself just staring at nothing for long stretches. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, even if part of you isn't sure this will help — that kind of ambivalence makes complete sense when you're grieving and feeling drained. Losing your grandmother and then trying to function at work while carrying that weight sounds genuinely exhausting, and those moments of blankness or losing your train of thought are often the mind's way of processing something too big to hold all at once. I'm wondering — when you say you don't think talking will change anything, what does "change" look like for you right now? What would feel like even a small bit of relief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess when I think about "change," I just mean... not feeling like I'm dragging myself through every single day, you know? Like, even getting through a meeting without zoning out and then panicking because I missed something important would feel huge right now. But I don't know how talking about my grandmother is going to make my brain actually work again at work.
therapist: What you're describing — just wanting your brain to feel like *yours* again — is such a real and valid goal, and it makes sense that the connection between grief and concentration feels unclear right now. The thing is, when we lose someone significant, our minds are often quietly working overtime in the background, which leaves very little room for the tasks we're trying to focus on. So talking about your grandmother isn't separate from the work struggles — it might actually be one of the most direct paths to feeling less like you're wading through mud every day.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that makes sense, but it still feels weird to me that talking about her could somehow fix my ability to concentrate at work. Like, those feel like two completely separate things in my brain — the sadness is over here, and the work stuff is over there, and I've kind of been trying to keep them that way on purpose. I think I was hoping you'd give me some kind of focus technique or productivity trick, not... this.
therapist: It's completely fair to want something concrete and practical — and we can absolutely work on that too. But I notice as you're describing keeping the sadness "over there" on purpose, there's something that sounds almost a little tender or tired underneath that, like maybe holding those two things apart has been taking more effort than it looks. I'm curious — how has that separation been working for you so far?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, I guess it has been kind of exhausting, if I'm being honest. Like I spend so much energy at work just trying to stay focused and professional, and then I get home and I'm just completely drained, but the loneliness is still right there waiting for me. I don't know if "separation" is even the right word — it's more like I'm just running from one thing to the next so I don't have to sit with it.
therapist: What you just described — running from one thing to the next so you don't have to sit with the loneliness — that takes an enormous amount of energy, and it sounds like you're starting to feel the cost of that. It's really meaningful that you named it so clearly just now, because that pattern of constant motion to avoid pain is often exactly what keeps us stuck and exhausted. What do you think it would feel like to actually let yourself sit with it, even just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, just the thought of sitting with it makes my chest tighten up. Like, if I stop moving, if I actually let myself feel how alone I am, I'm scared it'll just... swallow me whole, and I won't be able to function. I don't know if that makes sense, but stillness feels more dangerous to me than exhaustion does.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and what you're describing — that fear that feeling it fully will somehow consume you — is one of the most common and painful parts of grief. It's worth gently noticing that you've actually been sitting with some of this right now, in this conversation, and you're still here, still functioning, still finding the words. What if the feeling swallowing you whole is something your mind predicts will happen, rather than something that actually has?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess... yeah, I am still here, still talking. But I think part of me is worried that this is different from actually being alone with it at 2am when there's no one to anchor me. It feels safer right now because you're here, and I'm not sure I trust that I can hold it together when I'm on my own with it.
therapist: That distinction you're making — that it feels safer here because I'm present — is actually really important and worth holding onto, because it tells us something true: connection does help regulate us, and that's not a weakness, that's human. Those 2am moments alone with grief are genuinely harder, and I don't want to minimize that. But I'm curious — when you imagine yourself at 2am with those feelings, what do you picture yourself doing, and is there any part of you that has gotten through a moment like that before?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, I have gotten through those nights before, but honestly it doesn't feel like I "got through" them so much as I just survived them until morning came. Like I'd lie there scrolling my phone or staring at the ceiling, and eventually the sun would come up and I'd feel numb and exhausted but still here. I guess that counts, but it doesn't exactly feel like a victory — it feels more like I just waited it out, and I'm not sure that's the same as actually coping.
therapist: Surviving until morning — that *is* something, even if it doesn't feel like it, and I think part of you knows that, even as you're dismissing it. What strikes me is that you've done that more than once, which means there's something in you that keeps holding on even when it feels unbearable. I wonder if part of what we could work on together is building a bridge between just "waiting it out" and actually feeling like you have something to reach for in those moments — would that feel worthwhile to explore?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess... yeah, maybe there is something in me that keeps holding on, even though in those moments it feels more like stubbornness than anything meaningful. But when you say "something to reach for," I honestly don't know what that would even look like for me right now — it feels kind of abstract, like you're asking me to picture a color I've never seen. I'm not saying it's not worth exploring, I just... I don't want to get my hopes up and then feel even worse when it doesn't work.
therapist: That fear of hoping and then being disappointed makes so much sense, especially when you're already running on empty — hope can feel like a risk you can't afford right now. And I love that you called it stubbornness, because honestly, stubbornness kept you here through every one of those 2am nights, and that's not nothing — that's actually a real thing you can point to inside yourself. What if we didn't try to picture the whole color at once, but just got curious about one small thing that has ever made a 2am feel even slightly more bearable than another?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess... there have been nights where having my phone nearby helped, just knowing I could reach out to someone even if I didn't actually do it. But then I feel kind of pathetic about that, like I'm some grown adult who needs a security blanket just to get through the night. It's embarrassing to admit that something so small is what gets me through.
therapist: The fact that something so small has been quietly holding you together on the hardest nights isn't pathetic — it's actually you knowing yourself well enough to find what works. I'd gently push back on the word "embarrassing," because what you're describing is a completely human need for connection, and reaching for that, even symbolically, is the opposite of weakness. What do you think it says about you that even in your worst moments, some part of you wanted to stay close to the possibility of not being alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... when you put it that way, it does sound a little different than how I usually think about it. Like maybe there's a part of me that hasn't completely given up, even when everything feels impossible at 2am. But I'm not sure if that's strength or just desperation, honestly, because it doesn't feel like a choice so much as just... not knowing what else to do.
therapist: What you just said — that it feels less like strength and more like not knowing what else to do — I want to sit with that for a moment, because sometimes the most honest kind of holding on doesn't feel heroic, it just feels like the only option left. And your voice right now sounds quieter, a little more tender, like something softer is coming through underneath the words. I wonder if "desperation" and "strength" might not be as opposite as they feel — what if not giving up, even when you don't know why, is exactly what strength looks like when someone is exhausted and grieving?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
